name: British Columbia
summary_text: British Columbia stands under the Canadian framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation and hate-propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code, both carried by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia, and courts have applied these protections consistently. Sexual orientation has been a protected ground federally since 1996. No province or territory restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction for visitors.  British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation addressing trans people. It was the first jurisdiction in Canada to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code, in 1992, and is routinely assessed as the country's most progressive province on LGBT issues. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults; that ban applies in British Columbia.  Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Transgender people may change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, and federally issued identity documents can carry an X marker. Provincial human rights machinery is available to visitors and residents who face discrimination in the province.  National hate-crime data shows a mixed picture. A Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 covering police-reported hate crime in 2024 records 4,882 incidents, up 1% from 2023 after a 34% rise between 2022 and 2023, and a 169% increase since 2018, with the population rate down 2% to 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. The release breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, and it contains no British Columbia breakdown, so trans-specific hate-crime volume in the province is not established by this dataset.  Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the record. Federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed in correctional facilities according to their gender identity, and transgender prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Litigation has tested both placement and care: lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in a case over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns bear on a trans visitor only if the visitor is detained.

name: Manitoba
summary_text: Manitoba stands under the national framework: Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors, with gender identity and gender expression protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16 in 2017. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.  Provincially, the Manitoba Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The NDP government has a bill before the Legislative Assembly to extend the Code to gender expression as well. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe says the change would align Manitoba with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward presentation such as clothing. The bill was slated for debate later in 2025, and Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba, welcomed it. Until it passes, gender expression is not itself a listed prohibited ground in Manitoba, though conduct based on gender identity remains covered.  Manitoba's recorded hate-crime exposure is low by national standards. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, a 1% rise on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba recorded a rate of 5.3 per 100,000, joint-lowest among the provinces with Newfoundland and Labrador, and no increase in 2024, placing it among the eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly across the country, and police figures capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police. Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's reading of the same national police data, breaks out gender identity as a motivation alongside sexual orientation.  Provincial recognition of trans Manitobans is enacted and dated. The Legislative Assembly passed a bill on 30 May 2024 recognising March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.  The government also marks Transgender Day of Remembrance publicly. On 20 November 2023 the transgender flag was raised in Memorial Park in Winnipeg, an observance the province first held eight years earlier, with the flag raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara said in a statement that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia and that such violence shows no sign of slowing.

sources.title: Vriend v Alberta (1998) - Supreme Court of Canada
sources.documents: Held failure of a provincial legislature to include sexual orientation in human rights law violates s.15; led to all provinces, territories and federal government explicitly including sexual orientation and gender identity by 2017, including Manitoba.
